source.title: From Atoms to Trees: Building a Structured Feature Forest with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Yi-Fan Luo; Yang Zhan; Jie-Dong Jiang; Tian-Yang Liu; Ming-Rui Wu; Zhen-Nan Zhou; Bin Dong

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse-autoencoder feature extraction to LLM activations and reports feature interpretability results, extending indirect evidence about SAE-recoverable features to this hierarchical SAE method.
record.gate_note: Rows record Table 1 AutoInterp results, which directly assess the interpretability of SAE-extracted features. The paper's hierarchical-consistency metrics concern relations between features, not a listed claim version; other SAE benchmark scores are not recorded because they do not directly measure feature interpretability or recovery.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper proposing hierarchical SAEs (HSAE). It uses SAEs as a tool and reports its own method's benchmark scores against standard SAEs (Table 1, Table 3). AutoInterp here benchmarks SAE quality. It is not designed or framed as a test of whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features or of any other version. No toy models, neuron polysemanticity, completeness or dimensionality tests are run.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. HSAE recovers meaningful feature hierarchies and beats post-hoc baselines on hierarchy consistency. It also preserves standard SAE feature quality and reconstruction (comparable Table 1 scores).
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a jointly trained hierarchical JumpReLU SAE with parent-child constraints and feature perturbation; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that hierarchy consistency changes with the constraint weight, perturbation rate, tree assumptions, and hierarchy-update similarity metric; these results do not directly measure V4's feature-recovery claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Features learned at successive dictionary sizes (2048–16384) form parent-child relations with high co-activation. HSAE P(parent|child) is 0.769 vs 0.662 for post-hoc baseline SAEs at gemma2-2b layer 13. The authors read feature splitting as a hierarchy in the model rather than as non-canonicity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features across dictionary sizes are hierarchically organised (feature splitting reflects a conceptual taxonomy), relevant to whether dictionary features are canonical units.

record.problems: The V4 evidence is indirect and relies on AutoInterp scores from the main gemma2-2b layer-13 setup. The paper does not establish completeness or canonicality of the recovered features, and reports no uncertainty for these scores.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the directly relevant AutoInterp results. Other Table 1 benchmarks and hierarchy-structure results were not recorded because they do not directly measure the listed feature-recovery claim.

untested.parts: Toy models, sparsity-dependent transitions, geometry: not studied.
Capacity account of neuron polysemanticity: not studied.
Non-capacity origins of polysemanticity: not studied.
Distribution of features across neurons and recoverability of sparse features: not tested as a claim. SAEs are used as a tool and only benchmarked.
Completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE features: not measured. The authors only argue that feature splitting reflects hierarchy.
1-D vs multi-dimensional features: not tested. The linear representation hypothesis is cited only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V4' label was dropped. The rows compare the study's own method with standard SAEs and contain no test of whether superposed features exist or are recovered. AutoInterp scores of about 0.81–0.87 are reported without uncertainty or a chance baseline.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimension, overlap geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of capacity competition, including dedicated dimensions for important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The paper evaluates SAE feature interpretability in its main benchmark setting, but does not measure whether features are distributed across neurons, establish that SAE features are the model's underlying features, or report feature-interpretability scores across its additional model and layer settings.
Completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features is not directly tested.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional or multi-dimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: gemma2-2b layer 13 residual-stream activations; dictionary sizes 2048, 4096, 8192, and 16384
reader_labels.reason: The reported AutoInterp scores show that SAE dictionaries yield interpretable features in this setting; HSAE scores are 0.807–0.869 and baseline scores are 0.813–0.861 (A1–A8).
